paras.text: The Lahore Resolution was presented on 23 March and approved on 24 March. The Hindu newspapers published this resolution under the name “Pakistan Resolution”, although the word Pakistan was not used anywhere in the text of the resolution. The benefit of this was that an ordinary Indian Muslim faced no difficulty in understanding the aim of this resolution. If the Hindu press had not given it the name Pakistan Resolution, the Muslim leaders would have needed considerable effort to make the Muslims understand its aim and importance.

… took part. In these elections the performance of the Muslim League remained extremely disappointing. The Congress won a clear majority in eight Hindu-majority provinces out of eleven and formed its ministries. In none of these provinces did it give the Muslim League any share in the ministries. As soon as it came to power the Congress began implementing anti-Muslim policies, and the Muslims had to face all kinds of difficulties in the Hindu-majority provinces where the Congress was in government.

In September 1939 the Second World War began. The Congress decided to take advantage of Britain’s weakness during the war and presented a few demands to the British government; on their rejection the Congress ministries resigned in October 1939. The Quaid-e-Azam appealed to the Muslims to celebrate 22 December 1939 as a “Day of Deliverance”.

The Muslims had very bitter experiences during the period of Congress ministries in the provinces. They realised that after the departure of the British they would have to face even more difficulties at the hands of the Hindu majority in united India. In the light of these experiences the Muslims, instead of protecting their rights in united India, began demanding a separate and completely independent Muslim state.

The demand for the partition of India and a separate Muslim state was made by the Muslims from time to time, but this demand was made regularly for the first time in the form of a resolution in the annual session of the Muslim League held in Lahore in March 1940, which was named the Lahore Resolution.

This historic annual session of the Muslim League began in Lahore on 22 March 1940. On the first day of the session the Quaid-e-Azam, addressing a large gathering at Minto Park (present-day Iqbal Park), said that the problem of India is not of a communal but of an international nature. Until this basic fact is accepted, no constitutional structure will be workable here. The Quaid-e-Azam said: “The Muslims fulfil every definition of the word nation, and it is their right to have their own homeland, their own territory and their own state.”

On the second day of the session, i.e. 23 March 1940, the Chief Minister of Bengal, Maulvi Fazal-ul-Haq, presented that famous resolution which was named the Lahore Resolution.

Text of the Resolution

“It is the considered view of this session of the Muslim League that only that constitution is workable in this country, and the Muslims will accept only that constitution, whose basis is laid on the following principles: that geographically contiguous areas be demarcated into such regions, with necessary territorial readjustments, that the areas in which the Muslims are numerically in a majority, as in the north-western and north-eastern parts of India, be grouped together so that they may become independent states. The constituent units (provinces) included in these states shall be autonomous and sovereign.”

The Lahore Resolution was presented on 23 March and approved on 24 March. The Hindu newspapers published this resolution under the name “Pakistan Resolution”, although the word Pakistan was not used anywhere in the text of the resolution. The benefit of this was that an ordinary Indian Muslim faced no difficulty in understanding the aim of this resolution. If the Hindu press had not given it the name Pakistan Resolution, the Muslim leaders would have needed considerable effort to make the Muslims understand its aim and importance.

During the Second World War, in view of its war needs, the British government badly needed the cooperation of the people of India and its political parties. Under this need the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps to India on 23 March 1942 with a few constitutional proposals. دوسری جنگِ عظیم کے دوران حکومتِ برطانیہ کو اپنی جنگی ضروریات کے پیشِ نظر ہندوستان کے لوگوں اور یہاں کی سیاسی جماعتوں کے تعاون کی سخت ضرورت تھی۔ اس ضرورت کے تحت برطانوی حکومت نے سر سٹیفورڈ کرپس (Sir Stafford Cripps) کو چند نئی دستوری تجاویز کے ساتھ 23 مارچ 1942ء کو ہندوستان بھیجا۔ کرپس مشن کا ایک اہم مقصد ہندوستان کے عوام اور سیاسی جماعتوں کی خوشنودی حاصل کر کے انھیں جنگی کوششوں میں برطانوی حکومت کی مدد پر آمادہ کرنا تھا۔ سر سٹیفورڈ کرپس نے ہندوستان آمد کے بعد یہاں کے سیاسی راہنماؤں سے ملاقاتیں کیں اور 30 مارچ کو کرپس نے …
